THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF NON-

Statement 
(a) and (b) Solar lanterns were developed as a substitute for kerosene lanterns. 
They have been found to be very useful in rural and far-flung areas because of 
unreliable or lotal lack of power supply. In order to promote the use of solar lanterns in 
such areas. Government is implementing a countrywide programme for the supply of 
such lanterns on a subsidized basis. The subsidy is provided to non-commercial users of 
solar lanterns. For the current year, the admissible central subsidy per lantern is Rs. 1,300. 
For the North Eastern Region. the subsidy is 90% ex-works cost of the lantern 
subject to a maximum of Rs. 3.000. Other support measures taken by Government 
include reduction in customs duties on imported materials, exemption from excise duty 
and provision of loan assistance to manufacturers, intermediaries and non-
government organizations for promotion of solar lanterns. 
(c) The solar lantern programme is also being implemented in the states of 
Bihar. Ultar Pradesh and Uttaranchal. 42,149 solar lanterns have been distributed in 
Bihar (including Jharkhand) and 67.313 in Uttar Pradesh (including Uttaranchal) upto 31st 
March 2001. The following quantities have been allocated to these states for the year 
2001-02 :  
State Solar Lanterns 
Bihar 8.000 
Uttar Pradesh 10,000 
Uttaranchal 4.500 
(d) Docs not arise.

Prevention of Terrorist Activities Bill. 2000, which had earlier been put on the

overwhelming majority of the Chief Ministers of the States: and

consulted before introducing the Bill in Parliament ?

proposes to enact an effective anti-terr orism legislation. On a reference made 
in this regard by the Government, the Law Commission has drafted a Prevention 
of Terrorism Bill. 2000.

Administrations for soliciting their comments. Only a few States rejected outright 
38

Governments as well as the NHRC. which arc now available, and so modify the Bill that it

to be viewed as an integral part of an arrangement that prevent recurrence of 
similar defaults in future. The group has also recommended that the scheme

power projects. Some of the steps taken by the Government for 
simplifying and decentralizing the procedure for clearance of private 
power projects and to attract more  companies in the power sector, 
are : 
— minimizing the number of clearances required to be obtained for the 
purpose of appraisal of the private power projects by Central 
Electricity Authority (CEA). 
— minimizing the role of the Foreign Investment Promotion Boar.d by 
providing for automatic approval for foreign equity in selected 
categories and enlarging the provisions for automatic approval for such

and distribution have been permitted foreign equity participation up 
to 100% on the automatic approval route without any limit. 
— delegating more powers to State Governments for environmental 
clearance. 
— raising the capital cost limits up to which techno-economic clearance

reduction of time required for preparation.

Financial closure of I.P.P. 
4061. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH : Will the Minister of 
POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Union Government have pointed out that State 
Governments would have to assume responsibility for achieving financial closure 
of independent power projects; 
(b) if so, whether the Union Government has also pointed out that States would 
have to ensure financial closure of 16 major power projects before March 31st, 2001; 
(c) the total number of projects that are being considered for closure; 
(d) how many of such power projects have been closed; and 
(e) to what extent it has affected the power position ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER : 
(SHRIMATI J AYA WANTI MEHTA): (a) to (e) One of the main reasons for many 
Independent Power Producers not achieving financial closure is the inability of State 
Electricity Boards to offer an adequate payment security mechanism. With a view to 
identify an acceptable payment security mechanism for Independent Power Producers 
(IPPs), in the eighth meeting of the Crisis Resolution Group (CRG) held on March 
30,2000 under the chairmanship of Minister of Power, various alternatives to escrow 
were discussed, in this meeting, it was decided that financing of IPPs, from the 
concerned State Governments, should be linked with the progress of reforms 
undertaken by the State Governments. The Financial Institutions have agreed to 
undertake financing of IPPs on the basis of a legally binding agreement to be made 
by State Governments to provide escrow before Commercial Operation Date instead 
of the present practice of escrow at the time of financial closure. 16 power projects 
totalling 6887 MW were identified for removal of the Mast mile' problems by March 
31, 2001. Out of these, while one project [Surat 
119

Thermal Power Project (156 MW) of M/s Gujarat Mineral Development 
Corporation] has reported achievement of financial closure, six other projects 
with a total capacity of 2239 MW in Andhra Pradesh may achieve financial 
closure soon with the initialing of Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) among 
Government of Andhra Pradesh/APTRANSCO, Power Finance Corporation 
and the Financial Institutions led by the Industrial Development Bank of India 
on August, 10,2001. The remaining projects are closely monitored for removing 
the 'last mile' problems which would facilitate achievement of financial closure.

Scarcity of drinking water in flood hit areas of Orissa 
4073. SHRI ANANTA SETHI : Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government are aware of the severe scarcity of drinking water in 
the flood affected areas in Orissa; 
130 

|29th August. 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether any steps have been taken to ensure adequate drinking water 
supply to those flood hit areas: 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) whether any action plan has been initiated for those areas ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI SUBHASH MAHARIA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) As reported by the Government of Orissa, steps have been 
taken to ensure supply of drinking water to the flood hit areas. The State 
Government has opened Control Rooms at district, circle and State levels to 
monitor the flood relief works on war footing basis. The arrangement for 
providing drinking water in poly bags and through tankers to people who took 
shelter in highways and high lands after their dwellings were submerged has 
been made by Government of Orissa. Action for disinfecting the contaminated 
tube-wells, open wells including priv ate tube-wells with bleaching powder 
and calcium hypochloride has been taken soon after the flood water had receded. 
For this purpose. Government of Orissa has formed 186 mobile teams with 93 
mobile vans and 5 country boats. Halogen tablets were also distributed to the 
flood affected people for disinfecting the contaminated drinking water. 
Bacteriological tests were also carried out after disinfecting, to ascertain the 
efficacy of disinfecting. The unsafe sour ces were repeatedly disinfected. The 
tube-wells, which had gone out of order, were repaired and restored on 
emergency basis. 75298 tube-wells have been disinfected and 7648 tube wells 
have been repaired so far. 113 piped water supply schemes have been restored 
to normalcy. 
(d) As reported by the State Government, the following action plan has 
been initiated for supply of safe drinking water in the affected areas : 
(i) Supply of materials like bleaching powder, halogen tablets, calcium 
hypo-chloride solutions etc. have been kept ready to manage the 
calamity. 
(ii) New drinking water sources will be provided as per requirements. 
(iii) Sufficient spare parts have been kept ready for timely repair and 
maintenance. 
(iv) Regular tests will be conducted to ensure bacteriological safely of 
the source.

(b) and (c) No. Sir. The Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory Use in 
Packing Commodities) Act, 1987 (JPM Act) provides for compulsory use of 
jute in packaging of certain commodities in the interests of production of raw 
jute and sute packaging material, and of persons engaged in the production 
thereof, and for matters connected th erewith. The Act empowers the Union 
Government to direct from time to time that such commodity or class of 
commodities or such percentage thereof, as may be specified shall be packed 
for the purposes of its suppy or distribution in such jute packgaing materia! as 
may be specified.

year, after considering various factors like production of raw jute, production 
of foodgrains and sugar, interest of workers engaged in jute^griculture and jute 
industry and the consumers. At present there is no proposal to repeal the JPM 
Act. 1987.

(i) Customs duty has been reduced from 15% to 5% on 159 specified 
textile and garment machineries. In addition. 12 important items of machineries 
including shuttle less looms have also been exempted from additional excise 
duty. A programme has been announced to induct 50,000 shuttleless looms and 
to modernise 2.5 lakh power looms in the decentralised sector by 2004.

providing for a reimbursement of 5% out of interest, is available to the textile 
industry for modernisation and upgradatio n. In addition, rate of depreciation 
allowance for machinery under TUFS has been raised to 50%. 
(iii) A provision of Rs. 10 crores has been earmarked in the Budget 
2001-02 for the establishment of Apparel Parks for production and export of 
garments. Besides a provision of Rs. 15 crores has been made for the Scheme 
of improvement of critical infrastructure facilities at major textile production 
centres.

SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa): Sir, I cafl the attention of the

THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT. 
MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TE CHNOLOGY AND MiNISTER OF 
OCEAN DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLl MANOHAR JOSHI): Mr. 
Chairman. Sir. Hon Members have drawn my attention to the recent circulars 
of UGC and NCERT curriculum framework in the context of the National 
Policy on Education. 
The National Policy on Education (1986), as modified in 1992, was 
based on an indepth review of the entire gamut of the educational process. it 
enunciated a comprehensive framework to guide the development of 
191 

RAJYA SABHA [29 August, 2001] 
education in its entirety. It envisaged a National System of Education, which 
would be based on a national curricular framework containing a common 
core alongwith other flexible components. In the higher education sector, the 
policy provided for dissemination of specialised knowledge and skills, to 
make the system dynamic, constantly entering uncharted areas, redesigning 
courses and programmes to meet the demands of specialization better, etc. 
The NCERT has been established by the Government of India to 
assist and advise the Central and State Governments in all matters of school 
education. It engages in research and field studies and then comes up with 
programmes and activities which are con ducted in collaboration with States 
and other institutions.  The NCERT does not issue circulars. 
In response to the 1986 Policy, the NCERT has been contributing 
to the areas of universalisation of elem entary education (including the latest 
Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan), vocational education and introduction of educational 
technology, education of women, minorities and groups with special needs, 
teacher-training and research, surveys, st udies and innovations in the field of 
education, etc. 
In particular, during the recent past, the NCERT has implemented 
the following important programmes:- 
Setting up of the National Centre for Computer Education 
Setting up of National Centre for Value Education 
Setting up of the National Resource Centre for Inclusive education, 
for which UNESCO assistance is being sought. 
Setting up of Centre for International Relations for organizing 
training programmes for teachers and teacher-trainees for SAARC 
countries 
Revival of the Programme of Community Singing, initiated by Smt. 
Indira Gandhi in the early 1980s, but discontinued in the early 
1990S. 
While working in all these areas, the NCERT has been constantly 
responding to the new concerns and requirements emerging in curricular 
matters suitably. However, the need for reviewing and revising school 
curricula in the light of NPE - 1986, POA 1992 and the Ninth Five Year Plan 
document, was strongly felt which generated some projects for this purpose 
192 

[29 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
during the years 1996-97 and 1997-98. However, the progress was slow and 
it was re-energized in September, 1999. A Discussion Document on 
Curriculum Framework was published in January 2000, based on extensive 
deliberations/involvement of experts in its seven constituent units including 
the Central Institute of Vocational Studies, Bhopal and the Central Institute 
of Education and Technology, New Delh i and consultations with teachers. 
educators and parents. This was widely disseminated to State Education 
Ministers, all functionaries of state-level agencies dealing with school 
education, educationists, individual experts, non-governmental organizations, 
political leaders, newspaper editors an d journalists to initiate nationwide 
debate and consultation. It was widely covered by media and Press and was 
also put on the NCERT website. Seminars and conferences were also 
organized to discuss the document. 
Based upon the inputs received, NCERT has finalised the National 
Curriculum Framework in November, 2000. This was considered in 
December, 2000 in the General Body of the NCERT wherein all the 
Education Ministers of States/UT Governments are members. 
Copies of the final/revised document of the National Curriculum 
Framework for School Education were subsequently distributed to various 
organisations, Central/State Governments, Newspaper editors which include : 
all the Chief Ministers, 70  leaders of political parties, 55 State Education 
Ministers, 53 Education Secretaries, a large number of Education Experts and 
30 prominent Newspaper Editors. Besides, the National Curriculum 
Framework for School Education was discussed in two Conferences of State 
Education Secretaries held in November, 1999 and April, 2001, in both of 
which the Director, NCERT made a detailed presentation. 
Currently, NCERT is engaged in the task of developing new 
curricular materials including textbooks.   So far no such curricular materials 
have been finalised. 
The University Grants Commission is the apex body for promotion 
and coordination of university educa tion and for the determination and 
maintenance of standards of teachin g, examination and research in 
universities and colleges. 
The UGC has during the years 1999-2001 issued thirty-one circulars 
on excellence affe quality, covering comprehensive plan of action for 
improving the quality and standards of teaching and research, compulsory 
minimum attendance of 75 per cent by students. Universities of Excellence,

institutions, recognition of degrees specified by UGC, award Of degrees by 
private franchisees of universities, mi nimum standards of instructions for 
grant of first degree, appointment of observers in Selection Committees, 
Revised guidelines for Deemed Univer sities, listing of Fake Universities,

SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA (Tamil Nadu): Sir, thank you very much 
for giving me this opportunity to participate in this Discussion. On behalf of 
the AIADMK Party, I would like to put forth certain suggestions and opinions 
on the National Policy on Education. First of ail, I would like to say that I 
oppose the saffronisation of our educational policy. Our country is based on 
multi-lingual, multi-cultural and multi-re ligious approaches. The very word 
'saffronisation' of education policy indi cates that we are giving colour to 
education. Education is common to everybody, to every religion. So, 
education should not have any cotour; it should be as plain as water. Now, the 
Government has made an attempt to design a common and uniform education 
curriculum. Sir, as regards our educational status, our country stands in a 
notable place as compared to the other countries of the world. Sir, the Union 
Government has allotted 3.8 per cent of the GDP to education. But this is not 
sufficient. When we consider the situation prevailing in various States, we 
find that there are so many schools which do not have the basic facilities like 
building, laboratories or even the to ilet and drinking water facilities. The 
Union Government should consider all these things first, and it should help in 
giving financial aid to the State Governments to improve the basic education 
and it should also see to it that education is made compulsory in the primary 
stages.     In fact, to
